Capability
Productization Cycle

From a reusable service promise
to operation and improvement
A practical introduction · 25 minutes

slides.title: Start with the outcome people need

elements.text: A capability is a reusable ability offered to consumers, with an owner and a service promise.

items: Name the consumer and the job they need to complete.
Define what the producer provides and supports.
Choose the implementation after testing the need.

elements.alt: APIOps human scene illustrating that an API alone does not define a useful capability

elements.text: Example: let suppliers and service teams understand payment progress without repeated status enquiries.

slides.notes:
The method description explicitly avoids assuming implementation style in advance. A capability might be accessed through APIs, events, integrations or automation. This is not an organisational maturity assessment.

slides.title: Eight stations, revisited as evidence changes

elements.alt: Capability Productization Cycle route: strategy; consumer and producer requirements; architecture; solution and interaction design; delivery and operations; readiness; publishing and enablement; monitoring and improvement; feedback returns to earlier decisions

elements.text: Use the stations to expose missing decisions and evidence. Return to earlier work when assumptions change.

slides.notes:
The eight labels and their order follow the Capability Productization Cycle station mapping in method-data. This simplified route is an original presentation diagram, not the API Productization metro map. It does not prescribe a one-way delivery process.

slides.title: 1. Strategy: test one capability hypothesis

rows: Suppliers and service teams need to see payment progress.
Status is scattered; people contact support to explain delays.
Provide an authorised, current status and a clear next step.
Observe the journey, review enquiry reasons and test demand.
Proceed, revise or stop; name the capability owner.

elements.text: A reusable capability needs evidence of demand and an owner.

slides.notes:
Recommended strategy resources: Customer Journey Canvas, Capability Value Proposition Canvas, Capability Business Model Canvas and Capability Hypothesis Canvas. This table is a filled working summary, not the canonical canvas. Validate reuse with actual intended consumers.

slides.title: 2. Requirements: agree the service together

elements.text: Consumer and producer commitments

items: Consumer: describe use, access needs and change constraints.
Producer: define freshness, availability and support.
Owner: agree funding, scope and lifecycle decisions.
Together: test onboarding and the exception path.

elements.alt: APIOps human workshop scene representing agreement between capability consumers, producers and owners

elements.text: Example agreement: show the source timestamp; restrict access to permitted suppliers; explain unavailable status.

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Consumer & Producer Service Requirements. Use the Capability Consumer/Producer Requirements Canvas. Agree access, service, support, change and lifecycle commitments with all parties. The example is a proposed service expectation, not an SLA already agreed.

rows: A consumer needs current status now.

elements.text: Record the choice, alternatives, trust boundaries and operating cost.

slides.notes:

slides.title: 4. Design: make the service promise testable

rows: Define submitted, processing, paid and exception states.
Read current status; optionally subscribe to changes.
Identify caller and supplier; return only permitted records.
Distinguish unknown payment, delayed source and denied access.
Specify timestamps, version policy and consumer migration.

elements.text: Review the interaction with a real consumer before implementation.

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Capability Solution & Interaction Design. Recommended resources: Domain Canvas, Capability Solution Design Canvas, Interaction Canvas and contract-first design. Select the contract or service definition appropriate to the architecture; an OpenAPI contract only covers an HTTP API portion.

slides.title: 5. Delivery includes operation and support

items: Build one complete consumer path from access to useful status.
Test permissions, stale data, source failure and recovery.
Release with monitoring, support and rollback ownership.
Practise the incident and change process with the producer.

elements.text: Evidence to keep

items: Test results and release record
Runbook and escalation route
Dependency and access inventory
Recovery and lifecycle decisions

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Capability Delivery & Operations. Use implementation-style-appropriate engineering, testing, security, release, support and operational ownership practices. The Capability Readiness & Operations Canvas connects delivery decisions to operation. The numbered sequence is a suggested teaching workflow, not an additional mandatory method process.

slides.title: Use AI with agreed capability context

elements.text: Give AI the service promise, boundaries and reviewed interaction—not just a feature request.

items: Supply approved domain terms, contracts and acceptance examples.
Generate one small implementation or test change at a time.
Review permissions, failures and recovery with a human owner.
Run the applicable tests, linting and readiness checks.

elements.alt: Conceptual APIOps illustration of AI-assisted building with human review

slides.notes:
Author-developed guidance applying the delivery station to AI-assisted work; this is not a separate canonical capability station. For an API implementation, scaffold contracts, linting, tests and CI using the API tooling described in the technical deck. For integrations or workflows, use equivalent checks for those artefacts. AI output and a clean lint result do not establish service readiness. Do not put client secrets or restricted data in prompts.

slides.title: 6. Readiness: decide from evidence

rows: Reviewed service definition and consumer acceptance.
Failure tests, runbook, monitoring and fallback.
Can people use and support it?
Onboarding rehearsal, support route and named owners.
Recorded exceptions, accountable owner and review date.

elements.text: Release, release with accepted conditions, or return for more evidence.

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Capability Readiness Assurance. Use the capability readiness checklist, compliance/governance guide and service-quality checklist. Review design, contract or service definition, tests, operations, permissions, monitoring, support, fallback, lifecycle, risk and ownership. This is a teaching selection, not the complete canonical checklist.

slides.title: 7. Publish a capability people can adopt

rows: Payment progress for authorised suppliers and service teams.
Eligibility, request route, example interaction and first-use test.
Data freshness, supported usage and known limitations.
Capability owner, producer contact and escalation route.
Version, change notice, migration and retirement policy.

elements.text: Publishing includes enablement and support, alongside technical access.

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Capability Publishing & Enablement. Publish so intended consumers can discover, understand, request access, onboard, use and get support. Resources include publishing/discovery, consumer onboarding, service-agreement and versioning/lifecycle guides. Use a catalogue entry and service agreement appropriate to the selected style.

slides.title: 8. Measure value and improve the service

rows: Enquiry reasons and time to understand a delay.
Is the original problem being reduced?
Active intended consumers and repeat use.
Status age, failures and recovery time.
Cost to serve, support effort, dependencies.
Invest, change scope or plan retirement.

elements.text: Agree a baseline and review cadence; take findings back to earlier stations.

slides.notes:
Canonical station: Capability Monitoring & Improvement. Monitor value, outcomes, adoption, reuse, service health, consumer experience, cost, sustainability and lifecycle needs. Establish a baseline, data source, owner and review cadence before interpreting changes. Metrics above are proposals; no measured benefit or target is claimed.

slides.title: Choose a cycle view for the work ahead

rows: How it contributes to the same capability
Validate value, commitments, readiness and ongoing ownership.
Design and operate APIs selected as consumer interfaces.
Productize reusable connections between providers and consumers.
Design workflows, human controls, agents and exception handling.

elements.text: Keep one service promise and owner across implementation choices.

slides.title: Start with one capability and its consumers

items: Choose a consumer journey and write one capability hypothesis.
Agree the service promise with the owner, producer and consumer.
Compare implementation options and record the first decision.
Test a small service interaction and review readiness evidence.
Agree what to measure and when to revisit the hypothesis.

elements.text: Workshop output: an evidence backlog, named decision owners and a next review date.

slides.notes:
Suggested workshop facilitation sequence. Invite the capability owner, producer, intended consumers and architecture/operations representatives. Capture unknowns rather than inventing evidence. The method entry criteria are business goals defined and stakeholder approval; exit criteria are value proposition validated, architecture patterns validated, capability readiness confirmed and capability published for reuse.

slides.title: Make the next reuse easier

elements.text: A capability is ready for reuse when its value, service promise, access and operational ownership are clear.

items: Name one capability and the consumer outcome.
Find the weakest evidence across the eight stations.
Assign the next experiment and review the result.
